claim: The timing of sexually dimorphic differentiation of postmitotic, sex-shared neurons in the nervous system of the Caenorhabditis elegans male is controlled by the temporally regulated miRNA let-7 and its target lin-41.
source: The molecular mechanisms that control the timing of sexual differentiation in the brain are poorly understood. We found that the timing of sexually dimorphic differentiation of postmitotic, sex-shared neurons in the nervous system of the Caenorhabditis elegans male is controlled by the temporally regulated miRNA let-7 and its target lin-41, a translational regulator.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing effects of let-7 and lin-41 mutations on timing of sexual differentiation, including neurotransmitter switching and neuronal maturation.

claim: lin-41 acts through lin-29a, an isoform of a conserved Zn finger transcription factor, expressed in a subset of sex-shared neurons only in the male.
source: lin-41 acts through lin-29a, an isoform of a conserved Zn finger transcription factor, expressed in a subset of sex-shared neurons only in the male.
evidence: The manuscript provides genetic and expression data showing lin-29a is a target of lin-41 and is expressed specifically in male sex-shared neurons.

claim: Ectopic lin-29a is sufficient to impose male-specific features at earlier stages of development and in the opposite sex.
source: Ectopic lin-29a is sufficient to impose male-specific features at earlier stages of development and in the opposite sex.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that ectopic expression of lin-29a in AIM neurons induces male-specific neurotransmitter switching prematurely and in hermaphrodites.

claim: The temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of lin-29a expression is controlled intersectionally through the lin-28/let-7/lin-41 heterochronic pathway, sex chromosome configuration and neuron-type-specific terminal selector transcription factors.
source: The temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of lin-29a expression is controlled intersectionally through the lin-28/let-7/lin-41 heterochronic pathway, sex chromosome configuration and neuron-type-specific terminal selector transcription factors.
evidence: The manuscript provides genetic evidence showing that lin-29a expression requires heterochronic genes for timing, tra-1 for sex-specificity, and terminal selectors for neuron-type specificity.

claim: Two Doublesex-like transcription factors (mab-3 and dmd-3) represent additional sex- and neuron-type specific targets of LIN-41 and are regulated in a similar intersectional manner.
source: Two Doublesex-like transcription factors represent additional sex- and neuron-type specific targets of LIN-41 and are regulated in a similar intersectional manner.
evidence: The manuscript presents expression and genetic data showing mab-3 and dmd-3 are regulated by let-7/lin-41, tra-1, and terminal selectors in specific neurons.

claim: Most of the sex-specific features of the nervous system of C. elegans are established during postembryonic development.
source: Like in other animals, most of the sex-specific features of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans are also established during postembryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Barr et al., 2018; Sulston et al., 1980; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).

claim: The AIM interneuron class is glutamatergic in juvenile, pre-sexual maturation stages of both sexes, but during sexual maturation will turn off glutamatergic identity and turn on cholinergic neurotransmitter identity specifically in males.
source: For example, the AIM interneuron class is glutamatergic in juvenile, pre-sexual maturation stages of both sexes, but during sexual maturation will turn off glutamatergic identity and turn on cholinergic neurotransmitter identity specifically in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Pereira et al., 2015) and confirmed by data in the manuscript.

claim: Most if not all sexually dimorphic features of the C. elegans nervous system terminally differentiate during the fourth larval stage.
source: Most if not all of these sexually dimorphic features of the C. elegans nervous system terminally differentiate during the fourth larval stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Desai et al., 1988; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Pereira et al., 2015; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).

claim: Heterochronic genes do not control timing in all tissues, specifically not in gonadal maturation.
source: Such a role is not an obvious matter because heterochronic genes do not control timing in all tissues. For example, heterochronic genes are not involved in controlling the timing of gonadal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Euling and Ambros, 1996).

claim: Genome-wide association studies have linked one component of the heterochronic pathway to aberrant onset of puberty in humans.
source: Remarkably, genome-wide association studies have linked one component of the heterochronic pathway to aberrant onset of puberty in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review (Faunes and Larraín, 2016).

claim: Neither genetic removal of the germ cells nor laser ablation of gonadal precursor cells affects the execution of the AIM neurotransmitter switch.
source: We found that neither genetic removal of the germ cells nor laser ablation of gonadal precursor cells (which results in the loss of both gonad and germline) affects the execution of the AIM neurotransmitter switch (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from genetic and ablation experiments showing no effect on AIM neurotransmitter switching.

claim: In lin-28 null mutant males, the AIM neurotransmitter switch occurs prematurely.
source: However, we observed a premature onset of both unc-17/VACHT and cho-1/CHT expressions in AIM neurons of lin-28 mutant males (Figure 1B,D), mirroring the precocious cellular cleavage defects of lin-28 in epidermal tissues.
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-28 mutants showing premature cholinergic gene expression in AIM neurons.

claim: In males carrying a loss-of-function mutation in let-7, the neurotransmitter switch of the AIM interneurons is eliminated.
source: We also found that in males carrying a loss-of-function mutation in the miRNA let-7, whose processing is negatively controlled by lin-28 (Lehrbach et al., 2009), the neurotransmitter switch of the AIM interneurons is eliminated, that is, male AIM neurons remain glutamatergic (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in let-7 mutants showing AIM neurons remain glutamatergic in males.

claim: In lin-41 loss-of-function mutants, the neurotransmitter switch was prematurely executed.
source: We found that lin-41, the first of many let-7 targets to be identified (Slack et al., 2000) encodes this repressor factor. In lin-41 loss-of-function mutants (bch28), the neurotransmitter switch was prematurely executed
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-41 loss-of-function mutants showing premature neurotransmitter switching.

claim: In lin-41 gain-of-function mutants (xe8), the neurotransmitter switch of AIM was abrogated and AIM neurons remained glutamatergic.
source: while in lin-41 gain-of-function mutants (xe8), in which let-7 is unable to downregulate lin-41 activity due to a deletion of the let-7-binding sites in the lin-41 3'UTR (Ecsedi et al., 2015), the neurotransmitter switch of AIM was abrogated and AIM neurons remained glutamatergic (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-41 gain-of-function mutants showing AIM neurons remain glutamatergic.

claim: The L4-specific maturation of CEM neurons is precisely timed by the heterochronic pathway genes.
source: The heterochronic pathway genes also controlled the onset of differentiation of the male-specific CEM sensory neurons. Even though these neurons are already born in the embryo (and removed by apoptosis in hermaphrodites [Sulston et al., 1983]), the CEM neurons only fully differentiate at the fourth larval stage (Pereira et al., 2015). By analyzing the expression of cholinergic reporters, we found that this L4-specific maturation event is also precisely timed by the heterochronic pathway genes.
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in heterochronic mutants showing altered timing of CEM differentiation.

claim: The AIM neurotransmitter switch is entirely lost in lin-29 null mutants.
source: Consistent with lin-29 being a functional effector of lin-41 in the AIM interneurons, we find that the AIM neurotransmitter switch is entirely lost in lin-29 null mutants (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-29 null mutants showing loss of AIM neurotransmitter switching.

claim: The onset of differentiation of the male-specific CEM neurons in the L4 stage is unaffected in lin-29 null mutants.
source: In contrast, we found that the onset of differentiation of the male-specific CEM neurons in the L4 stage, as measured by the induction of cholinergic identity, is unaffected in lin-29 null mutants (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-29 null mutants showing normal CEM differentiation timing.

claim: lin-41 controls distinct effector genes in different neuron types.
source: These findings indicate that lin-41 controls distinct effector genes in different neuron types.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of lin-29 mutations on AIM versus CEM neurons.

claim: In the absence of mab-10, the AIM neurotransmitter switch and CEM cholinergic gene expression occurred normally.
source: However, analyzing the effects of a newly generated mab-10 null allele, we found that in the absence of mab-10, the AIM neurotransmitter switch and CEM cholinergic gene expression occurred normally (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in mab-10 null mutants showing normal AIM and CEM differentiation.

claim: mab-10 is not required for lin-29 function in AIM interneurons in males.
source: Hence, while mab-10 functions with lin-29 in seam cell differentiation, it is not required for lin-29 function in AIM interneurons in males.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal AIM neurotransmitter switching in mab-10 mutants.

claim: mab-10 expression initiates at the L4 stage in a ubiquitous manner.
source: We confirmed this notion by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated tagging of the mab-10 locus with mCherry, finding that ubiquitous mab-10 expression initiates at the L4 stage (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of endogenously tagged mab-10 showing L4-stage onset of expression.

claim: lin-28 is expressed very broadly in the nervous system in a sexually non-dimorphic manner and downregulated by the end of the L2 stage.
source: Consistent with previous reporter gene analysis (Moss et al., 1997), we found that a fosmid-based reporter construct of the lin-28 gene is expressed very broadly in the nervous system in a sexually non-dimorphic manner and downregulated by the end of the L2 stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of lin-28 reporter showing broad neuronal expression that is downregulated by L2.

claim: lin-41 shows broad expression in the nervous system from the L1 until the L4 stage in both sexes, when it becomes downregulated.
source: This lin-41 reporter allele showed broad expression in the nervous system from the L1 until the L4 stage in both sexes, when it becomes downregulated (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of endogenously tagged lin-41 showing temporal expression pattern.

claim: let-7 activity is temporally controlled in the nervous system.
source: We conclude that let-7 activity is, as expected, temporally controlled in the nervous system.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of let-7 activity sensor showing temporal downregulation at L4 stage.

claim: No sexual dimorphisms of lin-41 or let-7 sensor expression were observed in the nervous system.
source: We did not observe any sexual dimorphisms of lin-41 or let-7 sensor expression in the nervous system.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing similar expression patterns in males and hermaphrodites.

claim: The male-specific neuronal expression of lin-29 can be entirely ascribed to the a-isoform.
source: However, we found that this neuronal expression is almost completely restricted to the male and this male-specific expression can be entirely ascribed to the a-isoform (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of isoform-specific tagged alleles showing lin-29a is expressed in male neurons while lin-29b is not.

claim: The male-specific neuronal expression of lin-29a is not observed in male-specific neurons but is entirely restricted to sex-shared neurons.
source: The male-specific neuronal expression of lin-29a is not observed in male-specific neurons but is, interestingly, entirely restricted to sex-shared neurons (i.e. neurons that are generated in both sexes).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data identifying specific neuron types expressing lin-29a, all of which are sex-shared.

claim: 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes express lin-29a.
source: Specifically, 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes express lin-29a, including seven sensory neuron classes in the head and tail (AWA, ASG, ASJ, ASK, ADF, PHB, PLM), seven interneuron classes (AVA, RIA, AIM, AVG, RIF, PVC, PVN), a few head and tail motor neurons (SAB, PDA, PDB) and most of the sex-shared ventral nerve cord motor neurons (dorsal and ventral A, B and D-type and AS neurons).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data identifying specific neuron types expressing lin-29a.

claim: Expression of lin-29a in all these neurons in the male nervous system is precisely temporally controlled; it is first observed in the early L4 stage and persists throughout adulthood.
source: Expression of lin-29a in all these neurons in the male nervous system is precisely temporally controlled; it is first observed in the early L4 stage and persists throughout adulthood (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing temporal onset of lin-29a expression at L4 stage.

claim: The lin-29b isoform is expressed in three postembryonically generated touch neurons (AVM, PVM, PDE), where its expression is not temporally regulated and is observed in both sexes.
source: In addition to the male-specific neuronal expression of the lin-29a isoform, we also found that the lin-29b isoform is expressed in three postembryonically generated touch neurons (AVM, PVM, PDE), where its expression is not temporally regulated, that is, its expression is induced right after the neurons are born in the first two larval stages and expression is observed in both sexes (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation but notes data not shown.

claim: In lin-41(lf) mutants lin-29a::gfp expression is observed prematurely including in the sex-shared neurons of the male.
source: Indeed, we found that in lin-41(lf) mutants lin-29a::gfp expression is observed prematurely including in the sex-shared neurons of the male (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing premature lin-29a expression in lin-41 loss-of-function mutants.

claim: In let-7(lf) and lin-41(gf) mutants, lin-29a::gfp expression levels are significantly reduced compared to wild-type adult males.
source: As expected, in let-7(lf) and lin-41(gf) mutants (both of which maintain expression of LIN-41), lin-29a::gfp expression levels are significantly reduced compared to wild-type adult males (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing reduced lin-29a expression in let-7 and lin-41(gf) mutants.

claim: let-7-controlled LIN-41 directly represses lin-29a translation to control the precise timing of LIN-29A protein accumulation in the nervous system.
source: Together with our previous biochemical analysis (Aeschimann et al., 2017), we conclude that let-7-controlled LIN-41 directly represses lin-29a translation to control the precise timing of LIN-29A protein accumulation in the nervous system.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic data in the manuscript and cited biochemical analysis.

claim: In both lin-29a-isoform specific alleles (xe38 and xe40) the male-specific AIM neurotransmitter switch failed to occur.
source: We indeed find that in both isoform-specific alleles the male-specific AIM neurotransmitter switch failed to occur (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in lin-29a-specific mutants showing loss of AIM neurotransmitter switching.

claim: AIM-specific expression of lin-29a cell-autonomously rescues the neurotransmitter switch in lin-29a mutant males.
source: We found that in adult male animals, the loss of the AIM neurotransmitter switch (as assayed by cho-1 and unc-17 induction and eat-4 downregulation in AIM) is rescued by the transgene, thereby demonstrating cell autonomy of LIN-29A function (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents rescue experiment data showing cell-autonomous function of lin-29a.

claim: Ectopic expression of LIN-29A in AIM neurons causes premature neurotransmitter switching already by the first larval stage in males.
source: Examining juvenile males, before the onset of overt sexual maturation, we observed that the neurotransmitter switch is executed prematurely already by the first larval stage in these transgenic animals ectopically expressing LIN-29A in AIM neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in transgenic animals showing premature neurotransmitter switching.

claim: lin-29a is sufficient to induce the neurotransmitter switch in hermaphrodites.
source: Lastly, examining adult hermaphrodite animals expressing this construct, we found that lin-29a is sufficient to induce the neurotransmitter switch in the opposite sex (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data in hermaphrodites expressing lin-29a showing ectopic neurotransmitter switching.

claim: lin-29a is required and sufficient to control the AIM neurotransmitter switch.
source: We conclude that lin-29a is required and sufficient to control the AIM neurotransmitter switch.
evidence: This conclusion is based on loss-of-function, rescue, and gain-of-function experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: srj-54 fails to be expressed in AIM neurons in lin-29a mutants.
source: We found that srj-54 fails to be expressed in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6A) adding another AIM male-specific molecular feature that fails to be normally induced in the absence of lin-29.
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data showing loss of srj-54 expression in lin-29a mutants.

claim: lin-29a is required for dmd-5 expression in AVG neurons in males.
source: By analyzing the expression of a dmd-5 reporter in wild type versus lin-29a mutants, we found that lin-29a is required for dmd-5 expression in AVG in males (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data showing loss of dmd-5 expression in AVG neurons in lin-29a mutants.

claim: The induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons during sexual maturation in males is abrogated in lin-29a mutants.
source: Second, the daf-7 gene, encoding a neuroendocrine TGFβ-like signal, is turned on during sexual maturation in the sex-shared ASJ neurons only in males (Hilbert and Kim, 2017). This induction is also abrogated in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents reporter expression data showing loss of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons in lin-29a mutants.

claim: The PDB motorneuron grows elaborate branches off from its cell body and initial segment specifically in the male but not in the hermaphrodite.
source: Specifically, the lin-29a-expressing PDB motorneuron located in the pre-anal ganglion grows elaborate branches off from its cell body and initial segment of its posteriorly directed main process. This was only observed in the male but not in the hermaphrodite (Jarrell et al., 2012; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies and confirmed by imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: Male-specific PDB branches grow specifically during sexual maturation in the L4 stage.
source: We corroborated the existence and reproducibility of male-specific branches by visualizing PDB with a reporter transgene (Figure 6C). We found that these branches grow specifically during sexual maturation in the L4 stage (Figure 6C), co-incident with the onset of lin-29a expression.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing temporal onset of PDB branching at L4 stage.

claim: Growth of PDB branches is disrupted in lin-29a mutants.
source: Growth of these branches is disrupted in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging and quantification data showing reduced PDB branching in lin-29a mutants.

claim: lin-29a affects multiple distinct types of sexual maturation events, from gene expression to anatomy, in distinct neuron classes.
source: We conclude that lin-29a affects multiple distinct types of sexual maturation events, from gene expression to anatomy, in distinct neuron classes.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple experiments showing lin-29a effects on neurotransmitter identity, gene expression, and neuronal morphology.

claim: lin-29a mutant males do not display the obvious morphological and patterning defects displayed by the lin-29 null allele.
source: Critical for such an analysis is the fact that lin-29a mutant males do not display the obvious morphological and patterning defects displayed by the lin-29 null allele. Specifically, the male tail, whose overall morphogenesis is disrupted in lin-29 null mutants (Euling et al., 1999) appears morphologically normal in lin-29a mutants (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing normal male tail morphology in lin-29a mutants.

claim: No overt morphological differences were found between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males.
source: We precisely quantified other morphological differences between hermaphrodites and males using an automated visualization/measurement tool (Yemini et al., 2013) and found no overt morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative morphological analysis data showing no differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males.

claim: lin-29a mutant males were unable to mate.
source: In spite of spicule patterning appearing normal in lin-29a isoform-specific mutants, we observed that these mutants were unable to mate (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral assay data showing mating defects in lin-29a mutants.

claim: One aspect of mating behavior defective in lin-29a mutants is vulva location behavior.
source: We found that one aspect of mating behavior defective in these mutants is vulva location behavior (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral assay data showing vulva location defects in lin-29a mutants.

claim: lin-29a mutants are defective in mate searching behavior.
source: We indeed found that lin-29a mutants are defective in mate searching behavior (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral assay data showing mate searching defects in lin-29a mutants.

claim: The mate searching defects of lin-29a mutant males can be partially rescued by restoring LIN-29A expression exclusively in the AIM neurons.
source: Nevertheless, we could partially rescue the mate searching defects of the lin-29a mutant males by restoring LIN-29A expression exclusively in the AIM neurons (Figure 7D), indicating that lin-29a may function in several distinct neurons to control mate searching behavior.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral rescue experiment data showing partial rescue of mate searching by AIM-specific lin-29a expression.

claim: Adult male and hermaphrodites display distinct locomotor behavior when crawling on a lawn of bacteria.
source: It has previously been shown that adult male and hermaphrodites display distinct locomotor behavior when crawling on a lawn of bacteria (Mowrey et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: lin-29a mutants displayed a feminization of a number of body posture and locomotory features.
source: While many of them were not affected in lin-29a mutant animals (Figure 8 and Supplementary file 1), we found that lin-29a mutants displayed a striking feminization of a number of body posture and locomotory features.
evidence: The manuscript presents automated tracking data showing feminized locomotory features in lin-29a mutant males.

claim: lin-29a is required for the acquisition of male-specific postural and locomotory features.
source: Taken together, these results show that lin-29a is required for the acquisition of male-specific postural and locomotory features and that the absence of lin-29a results in a feminization of these behavioral parameters.
evidence: This conclusion is based on automated tracking data showing feminized behaviors in lin-29a mutants.

claim: Expression of lin-29a in the motor circuit rescued a defined subset of the feminized behavioral features (wavelength, crawling amplitude and midbody bend).
source: Expression of lin-29a in the motor circuit, using a cis-regulatory element from the unc-17/VAChT locus rescued a defined subset of the feminized behavioral features (wavelength, crawling amplitude and midbody bend) (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral rescue experiment data showing partial rescue of locomotory features by motor circuit-specific lin-29a expression.

claim: In tra-1(e1488) mutants, lin-29a expression becomes derepressed in XX animals.
source: We found that in tra-1(e1488) mutants, lin-29a expression becomes derepressed in XX animals (Figure 9A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing lin-29a expression in tra-1 mutant hermaphrodites.

claim: Nervous system-specific degradation of tra-1 by force-expressing fem-3 causes lin-29a expression to be derepressed in the hermaphrodite nervous system with the same pattern of cellular specificity seen normally in males.
source: Moreover, we induced the degradation of tra-1 exclusively in the nervous system by force-expressing fem-3, which promotes TRA-1 protein destruction (Starostina et al., 2007), under the control of a panneuronal driver. We found that lin-29a expression is derepressed in the nervous system of the hermaphrodite, with the same pattern of cellular specificity seen normally in males (Figure 9A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing lin-29a expression in hermaphrodites with nervous system-specific tra-1 degradation.

claim: The POU homeobox transcription factor unc-86 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AIM interneurons.
source: The POU homeobox transcription factor unc-86 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AIM interneurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of lin-29a expression in AIM neurons in unc-86 mutants.

claim: The LIM-HD transcription factor ttx-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in ASK.
source: The LIM-HD transcription factor ttx-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in ASK.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of lin-29a expression in ASK neurons in ttx-3 mutants.

claim: The COE/EBF transcription factor unc-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AVA, SAB, DA, DB, VA, VB, PDA, PDB and PVC neurons.
source: The COE/EBF transcription factor unc-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AVA, SAB, DA, DB, VA, VB, PDA, PDB and PVC neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of lin-29a expression in multiple motor circuit neurons in unc-3 mutants.

claim: The complex lin-29a expression pattern can be explained by an intersectional mechanism where temporal control is exerted via the heterochronic pathway, sexual specificity by the sex determination pathway and cellular specificity by terminal selector-type neuronal identity factors.
source: We conclude that the complex lin-29a expression pattern can be explained by an intersectional mechanism. Temporal control is exerted via the heterochronic pathway, sexual specificity by the sex determination pathway and cellular specificity by terminal selector-type neuronal identity factors.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic experiments showing requirements for heterochronic genes, tra-1, and terminal selectors for lin-29a expression.

claim: LIN-41 also represses mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA.
source: Previous whole animal RNA profiling of let-7 and lin-41 mutants, as well as RNA-binding assays demonstrated that LIN-41 also represses mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA (Aeschimann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous biochemical work.

claim: mab-3 is male-specifically expressed in the ADF neuron and additional head neurons, including the embryonically generated SMD head motor neurons.
source: Within the sex-shared nervous system, we found that mab-3 is not only male-specifically expressed in the ADF neuron, as previously reported (Yi et al., 2000), but also in additional head neurons, including the embryonically generated SMD head motor neurons (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of endogenously tagged mab-3 showing expression in specific neurons.

claim: Male-specific neuronal expression of mab-3 is precisely timed to commence at the L4 stage.
source: We found that like the male-specific, neuronal expression of lin-29a, male-specific neuronal expression of mab-3 is precisely timed to commence at the L4 stage (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing temporal onset of mab-3 expression at L4 stage.

claim: dmd-3 is expressed in PHC neurons and dmd-3::gfp expression in PHC commences at the L4 stage.
source: Similarly, the gfp-tagged dmd-3 locus is expressed in a sex-shared neuron class, the PHC neurons (Figure 9D), where dmd-3 acts to control the sexually dimorphic remodeling of PHC (Mason et al., 2008; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a). dmd-3::gfp expression in PHC also commences at the L4 stage (Figure 9D), at the time when PHC neurons remodel in a male-specific manner (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing temporal onset of dmd-3 expression at L4 stage in PHC neurons.

claim: The temporal specificity of nervous system expression of mab-3 and dmd-3 is lost in let-7 mutants.
source: We corroborated our previous data of LIN-41 protein affecting mab-3 and dmd-3 expression (Aeschimann et al., 2017) by showing that the temporal specificity of nervous system expression of mab-3 and dmd-3 is indeed lost in let-7 mutants (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in let-7 mutants.

claim: The male-specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in the nervous system is controlled by the tra-1 transcription factor.
source: Like lin-29a, the male-specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in the nervous system is controlled by the tra-1 transcription factor (Figure 9E,G)
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing ectopic mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in hermaphrodites with nervous system-specific tra-1 degradation.

claim: unc-42 is required for mab-3 expression in RMD and SMD neurons.
source: unc-42 is a terminal selector transcription factor that controls terminal differentiation of the RMD and SMD neurons (Pereira et al., 2015), and we found that mab-3 expression in these neurons fails to be induced in an unc-42 mutant background (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of mab-3 expression in SMD neurons in unc-42 mutants.

claim: ceh-14 is required for dmd-3 expression in PHC.
source: Similarly, ceh-14 is a terminal selector of PHC neuron identity (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a) and is required for dmd-3 expression in PHC (Figure 9F).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing loss of dmd-3 expression in PHC neurons in ceh-14 mutants.

claim: lin-41 operates through multiple distinct, male-specific effector genes and the temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of expression of these distinct effectors is controlled by a similar, intersectional regulatory logic.
source: We conclude that lin-41 operates through multiple distinct, male-specific effector genes and that the temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of expression of these distinct effectors is controlled by a similar, intersectional regulatory logic (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic experiments showing similar regulatory requirements for lin-29a, mab-3, and dmd-3 expression.

claim: Genetic manipulations in mice, as well as genome-wide association studies of humans with abnormally timed puberty demonstrate that lin-28 and let-7 also control timing of sexual maturation (puberty) onset in mammals.
source: Genetic manipulations in mice, as well as genome-wide association studies of humans with abnormally timed puberty demonstrate that lin-28 and let-7 also control timing of sexual maturation (puberty) onset in mammals (Chen et al., 2017; Corre et al., 2016; He et al., 2009; Ong et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2009; Sulem et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies in mammals.

claim: Mutations in human makorin, the orthologue of lep-2, a regulator of lin-28 activity in C. elegans, also affect the timing of puberty in humans.
source: This conclusion was further corroborated by the finding that mutations in human makorin, the orthologue of lep-2, a regulator of lin-28 activity in C. elegans (Herrera et al., 2016), also affect the timing of puberty in humans (Abreu et al., 2013; Bulcao Macedo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in humans and C. elegans.

claim: In the fly nervous system, lin-28 and let-7 are involved in controlling the timing of pupal to adult transitions.
source: Similarly, in the fly nervous system, lin-28 and let-7 are involved in controlling the timing of pupal to adult transitions (González-Itier et al., 2018; Sempere et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2012) that are accompanied by sexual maturation in the nervous system, as assessed by expression of the male-specific isoform of Fruitless, a master regulator of male-specific nervous system differentiation (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: LIN-29 is an ortholog of the uncharacterized vertebrate ZNF362 and ZNF384 proteins.
source: Orthology analysis with several tools (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017) as well as a detailed analysis of predicted DNA binding features suggests that LIN-29 is an ortholog of the uncharacterized vertebrate ZNF362 and ZNF384 proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on computational orthology analysis using multiple tools.

claim: The C. elegans nervous system may be even more sexually dimorphic than previously appreciated.
source: Some of the neurons that express LIN-29 or MAB-3 in a male-specific manner were not previously shown to display any sexual dimorphisms, demonstrating that the C. elegans nervous system may be even more sexually dimorphic than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is inferred from the discovery of male-specific expression of lin-29 and mab-3 in neurons not previously known to be sexually dimorphic.

claim: A ubiquitously expressed temporal coordinate system (heterochronic pathway) intersects with a ubiquitously expressed sexual coordinate system (sex determination pathway) to control the sexual and temporal specificity of a number of modular, neuron-type specific output systems that control sexual dimorphisms in distinct cellular circuit modules.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest a scenario in which a ubiquitously expressed temporal coordinate system (heterochronic pathway), intersects with a ubiquitously expressed sexual coordinate system (sex determination pathway) to control the sexual and temporal specificity of a number of modular, neuron-type specific output systems that control sexual dimorphisms in distinct cellular circuit modules (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of multiple genetic and expression experiments.

claim: This modular organization displays striking conceptual similarities with the modular organization of sexual dimorphic control mechanisms in vertebrates.
source: This modular organization displays striking conceptual similarities with the modular organization of sexual dimorphic control mechanisms in vertebrates (Yang and Shah, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of vertebrate sexual dimorphism mechanisms.

claim: The neuron-type specificity of the sex-specific regulator is controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selector transcription factors which define the overall differentiated state of individual neuron classes.
source: We provided evidence here that the neuron-type specificity of the sex-specific regulator is controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selector transcription factors which define the overall differentiated state of individual neuron classes (Hobert, 2016) (Figure 10B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic experiments showing terminal selectors are required for lin-29a, mab-3, and dmd-3 expression in specific neurons.

claim: There are several phylogenetically conserved binding sites for UNC-3 protein in the lin-29 locus.
source: Like the regulation of lin-29 by the temporal cue lin-41, the neuron-type specific regulation of lin-29 could potentially be direct since we noted several phylogenetically conserved binding sites for UNC-3 protein in the lin-29 locus.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the lin-29 locus for conserved binding sites.

claim: In the male AIM neurons, unc-86 and ceh-14 are required for the induction of unc-17 and cho-1 expression.
source: For example, in the male AIM neurons, unc-86 and ceh-14 are required for the induction of unc-17 and cho-1 expression (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Via the unc-86-mediated induction of lin-29 expression in the AIM neurons in males, unc-86 and ceh-14 are apparently able to induce, with the help of lin-29, the expression of unc-17 and cho-1.
source: Both are apparently not sufficient to induce unc-17 and cho-1 expression in hermaphrodites, but via the unc-86-mediated induction of lin-29 expression in the AIM neurons in males, unc-86 and ceh-14 are now apparently able to induce, with the help of lin-29, the expression of unc-17 and cho-1.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the genetic requirements for unc-86, ceh-14, and lin-29 in AIM neurotransmitter identity.

claim: The acquisition of AIM cholinergic identity during sexual maturation only in males was confirmed by analyzing the expression of the cholinergic unc-17/VACHT locus, tagged with mKate2 using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering.
source: The acquisition of AIM cholinergic identity during sexual maturation only in males was confirmed by analyzing the expression of the cholinergic unc-17/VACHT locus, tagged with mKate2 using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data of endogenously tagged unc-17 showing male-specific expression in AIM.

claim: Many of the LIN-29A expressing neurons are synaptically connected to one another.
source: Many of these LIN-29A expressing neurons are synaptically connected to one another (White et al., 1986) and some of the synaptic connections are known to be sexually dimorphic (Jarrell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The male-specific branches of PDB make extensive chemical and electrical synaptic contacts with both male-specific neurons, as well as sex-shared neurons.
source: These male-specific branches make extensive chemical and electrical synaptic contacts with both male-specific neurons, as well as sex-shared neurons (Jarrell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: PDB fails to make its branch-specific synaptic contacts in the absence of lin-29a.
source: These findings demonstrate a role for lin-29a in regulating the temporal and sexually dimorphic acquisition of male-specific neuronal morphologies and predict that PDB fails to make its branch-specific synaptic contacts in the absence of lin-29a.
evidence: This is predicted based on the loss of PDB branching in lin-29a mutants.

claim: The mate searching defects of lin-29a mutants are similar to the defects caused by loss of daf-7/TGFβ.
source: These defects are similar to the defects caused by loss of daf-7/TGFβ (Hilbert and Kim, 2017) and, consistent with this phenotypic similarity, we had described above that daf-7/TGFβ expression is lost in the ASJ neurons of lin-29a mutants.
evidence: This comparison is based on behavioral data in the manuscript and cited previous work.

claim: lin-29a may function in several distinct neurons to control mate searching behavior.
source: Nevertheless, we could partially rescue the mate searching defects of the lin-29a mutant males by restoring LIN-29A expression exclusively in the AIM neurons (Figure 7D), indicating that lin-29a may function in several distinct neurons to control mate searching behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of mate searching by AIM-specific lin-29a expression.

claim: The locomotory phenotypes in lin-29a mutants are the result of neuronal defects rather than being a secondary consequence of overall body morphology.
source: The lack of morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males indicates that these locomotory phenotypes are the result of neuronal defects rather than being a secondary consequence of overall body morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of morphological defects in lin-29a mutants despite locomotory defects.

claim: Other lin-29a-expressing neurons may be involved in controlling locomotory and postural features not rescued by motor circuit-specific lin-29a expression.
source: Other lin-29a-expressing neurons may be involved in controlling locomotory and postural features not rescued by this transgene.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of locomotory features by motor circuit-specific lin-29a expression.

claim: A previously described upstream regulator of lin-28, the lin-4 miRNA, does not affect male-specific sexual maturation in the nervous system.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a previously described upstream regulator of lin-28, the lin-4 miRNA (Moss et al., 1997), does not affect male-specific sexual maturation in the nervous system, suggesting the existence of alternative pathways that determine when lin-28's function in controlling let-7 processing is downregulated.
evidence: The manuscript states that lin-4 mutants show no defect in timing of CEM differentiation and AIM neurotransmitter switching.

claim: LEP-2/Makorin-mediated LIN-28 degradation is another means to control lin-28 function.
source: Recent work in C. elegans has discovered LIN-28 protein degradation, mediated by the conserved LEP-2/Makorin protein, as another means to control lin-28 function (Herrera et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The regulation of lin-29 by terminal selectors could potentially be direct.
source: Like the regulation of lin-29 by the temporal cue lin-41, the neuron-type specific regulation of lin-29 could potentially be direct since we noted several phylogenetically conserved binding sites for UNC-3 protein in the lin-29 locus.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of conserved binding sites in the lin-29 locus.
